articles.title: Isaac, a cat missing since the Brooklyn building collapse, has been reunited with his young owner
articles.description: Isaac, a cat missing since the Brooklyn building collapse, has been reunited with his young owner AP News Teen reunites with cat that went missing during Brooklyn building collapse after emotional plea CBS News Zariah, 13, and Her Cat Are Reunited After Building Collapse The New York Times Isaac, a cat missing since Brooklyn building collapsed, is reunited with owner NBC News Girl’s joy as crews find cat a week after
articles.content: NEW YORK (AP) — A cat missing since last week’s deadly Brooklyn building collapse has been found alive and reunited with his young owner, New York City officials said Sunday. Allie Taylor, director of the Mayor’s Office of Animal Welfare, said her office worked with the veterinary nonprofit Flatbush Cats to locate Isaac and reunite him with 13-year-old Zariah Coleman. It was a bit of good news amid the tragedy of Wednesday’s collapse, which killed eight people, injured 18 others and forced the evacuation of several nearby buildings, including one next door where Zariah lives. Zariah and her mother told The New York Times on Sunday that workers found Isaac on Sunday in a cabinet under the kitchen sink of Zariah’s apartment after hearing a soft meow. Zariah and her family hadn’t been allowed in since the collapse, which tore off the side of her building and left a hole where her bedroom wall had been. Waiting outside, Zariah hugged the cat’s cage as workers brought him out of her apartment building. Isaac had gone four days without food or water. After his rescue, he was taken to Flatbush Cats’ veterinary clinic for a checkup. “I had it in my heart they would find Issac,” Zariah told the Times. “I knew they would.” Zariah tearfully spoke about her missing cat at a news conference on Friday, telling reporters: “I just really hope they come and get our cat. He’s hiding from them, and I think he’s scared.” Mayor Zohran Mamdani heralded Isaac and Zariah’s reunion in a social media post. He thanked Taylor’s office, the city’s Buildings Department and the nonprofit for the happy outcome. “Isaac is now receiving the veterinary care he needs,” Mamdani said. “We’re grateful to everyone who helped bring them back together.”

Apple launches new app to study how people use AI for health
articles.description: Apple's new app for a study will answer everyday medical questions
articles.content: Big AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have made their bets on offering chatbots that can answer health-related queries with specialized features. Apple is debuting a new study to understand how people use AI for health. But it isn’t quite following other AI startups just yet; it wants to study how clinically grounded answers can help people. The iPhone maker is partnering with healthcare-focused AI company OpenEvidence to launch a new study app. Apple is inviting users in the U.S. over 21, using iPhone 15 or later, and running iOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled. The company is aiming to run this study with up to 200,000 participants for more than 12 months. The new app will allow users to ask health-related questions, as they do with ChatGPT or Claude, with answers grounded in clinical data, from sources including The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature. Apple said that the app will try to give simplified answers to everyday medical questions. Users can rate those answers and provide feedback about the responses; they’ll also be asked to participate in monthly surveys. Participants can share data from HealthKit such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep, or lab results to get more personalized and pointed suggestions from the app. The company said the app can also help prepare participants better for a doctor’s visit, and it will guide users to specific providers for answers related to concerning medical issues. Apple specified that the data will be anonymized before sending it to a secure third-party cloud provider, and it won’t be used to train any kind of AI models. The company said that OpenEvidence deletes the query and response data after 24 hours. “At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement, adding, “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.” The app is available to download starting today for U.S. users. It’s not clear if Apple wants to release AI-powered answering to its Health app or Siri yet. The potential is huge — earlier this year, OpenAI said users were asking over 300 million health-related queries each week. articles.content: Apple announced a new study today with the goal of better understanding how people interact with conversational AI health tools and how useful their responses actually are. The company is conducting the Apple Health AI Usage Study in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform used by healthcare professionals that generates answers based on medical information from sources like The New England Journal of Medicine. Participants will use a new iOS app to ask medical questions and then rate the responses based on criteria including accuracy, detail, and relevance. The app is now available for download, and enrollment starts today, with Apple looking for up to 200,000 people to contribute. Participants 21 and older must be based in the US, and although the app doesn’t use Apple Intelligence, it does require an iPhone 15 Pro running iOS 26 or later. Study participants can use the app to ask health-related questions and receive easily understandable responses with links to peer-reviewed clinical sources. The app relies on text-based prompts, and while dictation is an option using the iOS keyboard, the app isn’t integrated with Siri or Apple Intelligence. [Image: Participants in the study will be given the opportunity to rate responses to health questions from the app. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/applestudy2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] During enrolment, participants are given the option to share Apple HealthKit data, like their activity, sleep, or clinical lab results, so responses will include more context about their own personal health. But privacy is a priority, and Apple says it has taken measures to ensure users’ information remains confidential and the data collected won’t be used to train AI models. The aim is to improve the design and functionality of AI-powered health tools so they can deliver relevant health information that’s easier for users to understand and act on. “At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life. Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey,” said Sumbul Desai, MD, Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness.

articles.title: Fox's 'Big Noon Saturday' at Ferris State for first D-II broadcast
articles.content: Ferris State is getting the national college football spotlight - and making history in the process. FOX Sports' "Big Noon Kickoff" will broadcast live Saturday from Top Taggart Field in Big Rapids, marking the show's first-ever visit to a Division II school. It comes as the Bulldogs head into the opening round of the NCAA Division II Playoff Game against Truman State (Mo.), according to Ferris State University Athletics. "Big Noon Kickoff is a high energy, on campus pregame party and TV show, perfect for fans who want to be part of the action before kickoff," officials wrote Sunday. "It has become one of FOX's flagship college football programs, anchoring its strategy around the highvisibility noon kickoff window." College GameDay: ESPN College GameDay coming to Kalamazoo for WMU Football Fans are invited to attend the show, which is slated to run from 10 a.m. to 12 p.m. Admission will be free on a first come, first serve basis. Fans are encouraged to wear their school colors and bring signs - with the most creative potentially winning a prize, officials said. A variety of special promotions and opportunities to win are expected to be announced throughout the week, according to Ferris State University Athletics. Storm Ready: Watch News Channel 3's Winter Weather Special "Big Noon Kickoff" is a premier, traveling pre-game studio show broadcast by FOX from major college campuses across the country. More information about the show can be found online.

articles.content: The U.S. Department of Energy has issued a seventh consecutive 90-day emergency order keeping the coal-fired J.H. Campbell plant in Port Sheldon Township available to operate through mid-February — despite a recent federal appeals court ruling striking down the original directive. [Brian Vernellis/ONN]This story was originally published by Ottawa News Network. PORT SHELDON TWP. — The U.S. Department of Energy has issued a seventh consecutive 90-day emergency order keeping the coal-fired J.H. Campbell plant in Port Sheldon Township available to operate through mid-February — despite a recent federal appeals court ruling striking down the original directive. The new order, issued late Friday, Nov. 13, took effect Sunday, Nov. 15, and runs through Feb. 12, 2027. It instructs the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, or MISO, and Consumers Energy to maintain the 1,420-megawatt facility’s operational readiness for emergency grid needs while using economic dispatch to limit ratepayer costs. Operating along the Lake Michigan shoreline since 1962, the 64-year-old plant had been slated to burn its final ton of coal on May 31, 2025 — roughly 15 years ahead of the end of its scheduled design life — under a 2022 state-approved clean energy transition plan expected to save ratepayers roughly $600 million by 2040. Instead, just eight days before decommissioning, federal officials intervened with the first of several 90-day mandates. Keeping the aging facility running past its planned closure has added roughly $640,000 to $1 million per day in unbudgeted coal deliveries, maintenance and compliance costs, accumulating between $259 million and $295 million in extra expenses as of September 2026, according to federal court filings and estimates from state officials. Read More: Cost of the Campbell: How a West Michigan coal plant became the epicenter for a U.S. energy war U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in the latest order that keeping dispatchable coal generation active remains necessary to prevent winter blackouts across the region. “President Trump and the Energy Department remain committed to doing everything in our power to stop power outages for American families and businesses,” Wright said. “Ensuring coal plants such as the Campbell Plant are available to operate has prevented blackouts and likely saved lives. Americans deserve access to affordable, reliable, and secure electricity regardless of whether the wind is blowing or the sun is shining.” According to the DOE, ongoing reliability strains mirror events observed earlier this year. Officials pointed to a joint report from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and the North American Electric Reliability Corporation analyzing the Winter 2026 Arctic Cold Period — including Winter Storm Fern, during which MISO declared energy emergency alerts and Campbell generated more than 201,000 megawatt-hours of electricity. Before federal officials intervened in May 2025, the debate over the J.H. Campbell plant’s future played out inside the Ottawa County Board of Commissioners’ boardroom. [ONN file] Local political backdrop, community protests Before federal officials intervened in May 2025, the debate over the plant’s future played out inside the Ottawa County Board of Commissioners’ boardroom, exposing local political divides over grid reliability and environmental impacts. As reported by the Ottawa News Network, far-right Ottawa Impact commissioners pushed in early 2025 for the county to sue Consumers Energy to halt the shutdown — and some community members floated having the county take over the facility as a public utility. While the full board rejected a lawsuit 7-4, commissioners voted 9-1 in February 2025 to approve a nonbinding resolution authored by then-Vice Chair Josh Brugger urging state regulators and the utility to pause the closure and review grid conditions. “There was a concern by some constituents that the plant was going to close and they wanted it to stay open. There were also concerns by other members of the community who were concerned that it might stay open, and they wanted it to be closed for environmental issues among other things, so that came to the fore very quickly in 2025,” Brugger, who is now the board’s chair, told ONN earlier this year. Reflecting on the board’s decision to weigh in on state and federal energy policy, Brugger added: “We felt, in the end, that we were kind of closest to the area of concern and so perhaps we had a different perspective. In hindsight, I’m not sure that we did, but that’s what we felt, and we felt we had an obligation to do that.” Once the federal mandates took effect, frustration across Ottawa County spilled out of meeting rooms and into the streets through a series of rallies and demonstrations. Ahead of the first 90-day order’s expiration, environmental advocates, medical professionals and local residents — organized by the Michigan League of Conservation Voters and the Sierra Club Michigan Chapter — gathered outside the gates of the Port Sheldon Township facility on Aug. 12, 2025, alongside state Rep. Stephen Wooden, D-Grand Rapids, and former Ottawa County Commissioner Chris Kleinjans. Read More: Activists, officials call for closure of Campbell coal plant as utility looks to recover costs Read More: Protestors rally in Holland, call for Campbell coal plant to close Speakers warned about respiratory health risks from sulfur dioxide and particulate emissions, with Grand Haven-area resident Jeffrey Miller telling local media that keeping the plant open made no sense “financially, politically, economically, environmentally.” Three days later, on Aug. 15, 2025, roughly 100 residents and youth activists assembled at Memorial Park and Window on the Waterfront in downtown Holland, marching to U.S. Rep. Bill Huizenga’s district office to demand an end to the federal coal mandate and criticize rising utility costs. On May 21, 2026 — marking one year since Wright issued the initial emergency order — Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel held a press conference directly outside the Campbell plant to condemn the continued extensions and highlight mounting costs passed on to ratepayers. Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel mark the one-year anniversary since the U.S. Department of Energy issued an emergency order forcing the J.H. Campbell plant to remain open on May 21, 2026. [ONN file] Legal challenges, environmental concerns The latest federal directive arrives two months after a unanimous panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit ruled on Sept. 11 that the DOE overstepped its statutory authority under Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act when it blocked the plant’s May 2025 retirement. Writing for the court, Circuit Judge Cornelia Pillard held that Section 202(c) emergency powers apply only when the agency identifies “a risk of substantial harm from inadequate electricity supply that calls for immediate action by DOE in particular,” rather than long-term resource adequacy concerns managed through state and regional planning. “Permitting DOE to compel generation in a situation that can be resolved through the ordinary resource adequacy planning mechanisms … would render meaningless the constraints on federal power that Congress imposed throughout the Act,” the court wrote, warning that the department’s interpretation “would empower it to pick its preferred power sources in Michigan — or, presumably, any other state — and order them to operate” and “invites frequent federal interventions that are unsupported by the statute and threaten the stability of the energy market.” In its Nov. 13 order, the Energy Department noted it has petitioned the D.C. Circuit for a full-court rehearing and continues to invoke its emergency authority. Michigan officials, health professionals and environmental advocates have sharply criticized the repeated extensions, arguing the orders unlawfully override state regulatory planning while driving up electricity bills and prolonging air and water pollution along the Lake Michigan shoreline. Continued coal combustion emits sulfur dioxide, nitrous oxides and air particulates while adding to coal ash ponds and wastewater discharges that local residents worry threaten groundwater and Lake Michigan. Nessel, who led the multistate legal challenge alongside environmental groups including the Environmental Law & Policy Center and the Natural Resources Defense Council, said in September that keeping the aging facility open had already cost $295 million. “By forcing its continued operation, DOE tried a never-before-used tactic to illegally prop up the aging J.H. Campbell coal plant that nobody asked to keep, sticking ratepayers with a bill for a facility that should have been retired more than a year ago,” Nessel said in a statement challenging the federal orders. Following September’s appellate victory, Environmental Law & Policy Center leaders emphasized that state regulators and utilities had already planned for reliable replacement power. “No community should be forced to keep dirty, uneconomic coal power plants open when affordable clean energy solutions are readily available,” the group stated, adding that Michigan had already committed to a clean energy transition and that federal agencies should not interfere with state-approved resource plans. Utility response, ratepayer impact Consumers Energy — which did not request the emergency orders and has added 1,200 megawatts of generating capacity elsewhere in West Michigan to offset the planned retirement — confirmed it will continue complying with the federal mandate while seeking regional cost recovery so Michigan customers do not shoulder the entire expense alone. Because the plant operates under a federal mandate rather than standard market economics, net operating losses — which Consumers Energy reported exceeded $135 million in net excess operational costs earlier this year out of nearly $260 million to $295 million in total gross operating and compliance expenses — are passed on to ratepayers across MISO’s 15-state regional grid footprint. “Consumers Energy will continue to follow the law and operate our Campbell plant in West Michigan, complying with the seventh 90-day emergency order from the U.S. Department of Energy,” the utility said in a statement to WZZM-13 on Saturday, Nov. 14. “Consistent with these emergency orders, we will work to ensure that everyone who benefits from power from the Campbell plant across the Midwest pays their fair share.” Once federal mandates expire and decommissioning formally begins, Consumers Energy expects the remediation and restoration process at the Port Sheldon Township site to take roughly five years. — Sarah Leach is the executive editor of the Ottawa News Network. The King’s Trust and OpenAI launch £1m partnership
articles.description: The King’s Trust and OpenAI launch a £1m partnership to help up to 25,000 young people across the UK build practical AI skills for work.
articles.content: The new partnership will help young people build AI skills for the future workforce, prioritizing those not in education or employment. The King’s Trust(opens in a new window) has announced a major partnership with OpenAI designed to help up to 25,000 young people build AI skills for work, prioritizing those not in education, employment or training. OpenAI is making a £1m donation to the youth charity to support this work. This is part of a wider program of nationally recognized AI qualifications that The Trust will launch in the coming months, designed to help young people stay ahead of a changing labor market. The announcement comes as The King’s Trust marks its 50th year and looks to the future, helping ensure young people are supported to succeed in an increasingly AI-enabled world. The King’s Trust and OpenAI have launched a £1 million partnership to help young people across the UK build AI skills for work, prioritizing those who are not in education, employment or training (NEET). The program aims to support up to 25,000 young people over the next 18 months, helping them develop practical skills and confidence to move toward education and employment in an AI-enabled economy. The program will help address a gap in young people’s experience of AI while responding to their appetite to learn. The Open University’s Business Barometer 2026(opens in a new window) found that 68% of 16–24-year-olds surveyed who were not in education, employment or training would be willing to train or upskill to improve their job prospects. The partnership will help prepare young people for the opportunities and challenges of a rapidly changing world of work by combining opportunities to learn AI skills with recognized qualifications and practical experience. It forms part of a wider program of nationally recognized AI qualifications being developed by The King’s Trust, designed to equip young people with the skills employers need as AI transforms the world of work. Working with employers, AI specialists and young people, The King’s Trust is exploring the skills young people will need in a world of work where AI is becoming part of everyday life, and how these can complement the employability skills already embedded across its programs. Building on a 50-year legacy of supporting more than 1.3 million young people, The King’s Trust wants to ensure the next generation gains the skills and confidence needed to thrive in an AI-enabled economy. Ahead of the final report of the independent Young People and Work review, the Rt Hon Alan Milburn welcomed the partnership, reflecting on the shared ambition to improve young people’s opportunities to learn and earn. For OpenAI, the partnership forms part of a broader commitment to helping young people develop the skills and confidence to benefit from AI. It builds on wider efforts to make practical AI learning more accessible, including through OpenAI Academy, which provides free learning resources for students, job-seekers and other learners.

articles.title: Indian chip startup Bharat Semi lands $24M seed round as it eyes global AI sensor market
articles.description: Bharat Semi says it has secured design wins for its AI-enabled sensor technology with companies including General Atomics.
articles.content: Bharat Semi, an Indian semiconductor startup, has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors, as it seeks to win customers in the United States and elsewhere. The investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup says it has secured design wins with U.S. defense technology company General Atomics and India’s Kaynes Semicon. Its image sensors, however, remain under development, with the startup targeting its initial commercial production in 2027. India has committed billions of dollars to build up a domestic semiconductor industry, with a hope to become an alternative manufacturing hub as U.S. companies look to diversify supply chains beyond China. The country, however, has yet to establish itself as a major chip manufacturing hub. Meanwhile, the AI boom is also giving Indian startups such as Bharat Semi an opportunity to develop specialized chips for global markets. The New Delhi-based startup is developing programmable image sensors that combine image capture, processing, and AI capabilities on a single chip, reducing the need to send visual data to separate processors. The move could cut system costs by at least 70% compared with conventional setups that use a separate image sensor, image signal processor, and a system-on-chip, co-founder Vrinda Kapoor (pictured above, right) said in an interview. “Our aim here is to move from sensors to sense-making solutions,” Kapoor told TechCrunch. Kapoor, a South Park Commons fellow who earlier worked in healthcare technology, co-founded Bharat Semi in late 2021 with Vinayak Dalmia (pictured above, left), the startup’s managing director, who previously worked at McKinsey and in private equity. Its chief technology officer, Boyd Fowler, previously held the same role at image-sensor maker OmniVision. Bharat Semi is targeting smart homes, industrial automation, surveillance, and aerospace. Without disclosing specifics, Kapoor pointed to air conditioners that could detect when a room is empty and adjust automatically and drones that could process visual information — even with the absence of more expensive computing hardware elsewhere in the system. The startup’s first-generation sensors are already in prototyping, while its second-generation sensors, which will incorporate more advanced AI capabilities, are expected to reach the prototype stage by mid-2027, Kapoor said. Moreover, the startup plans to get those newer sensors into customers’ hands by the end of 2027. The all-equity seed round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons, and Indus Bridge Ventures, with participation from Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels, and individual investors. Bharat Semi, Kapoor said, plans to use the funding to expand its engineering team, complete product development, and bring its sensors to market. Bharat Semi has about 75 employees across India and the U.S., including 10 to 12 in its American operations, which span engineering and business development in Santa Clara. The startup plans to increase its U.S. headcount to around 20 by mid-2027, Kapoor said. It has also begun hiring engineers in Europe. “It’s a story of can we build a global technology company out of India,” Kapoor said. In 2024, Bharat Semi announced plans for a semiconductor fabrication project in India involving a technology partnership with the U.S. Space Force. The initiative, Kapoor said, remains in development and the startup is working to identify domestic partners that would build and operate the facility. The project is separate from Bharat Semi’s image-sensor business, Kapoor added. The startup plans to remain fabless, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on semiconductor design and software. The new funding will not be used to finance the proposed fabrication facility. articles.content: Bharat Semi, an Indian semiconductor startup, has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors, as it seeks to win customers in the United States and elsewhere. The investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup says it has secured design wins with U.S. defense technology company General Atomics and India’s Kaynes Semicon. Its image sensors, however, remain under development, with the startup targeting its initial commercial production in 2027. India has committed billions of dollars to build up a domestic semiconductor industry, with a hope to become an alternative manufacturing hub as U.S. companies look to diversify supply chains beyond China. The country, however, has yet to establish itself as a major chip manufacturing hub. Meanwhile, the AI boom is also giving Indian startups such as Bharat Semi an opportunity to develop specialized chips for global markets. The New Delhi-based startup is developing programmable image sensors that combine image capture, processing, and AI capabilities on a single chip, reducing the need to send visual data to separate processors. The move could cut system costs by at least 70% compared with conventional setups that use a separate image sensor, image signal processor, and a system-on-chip, co-founder Vrinda Kapoor (pictured above, right) said in an interview. “Our aim here is to move from sensors to sense-making solutions,” Kapoor told TechCrunch. Kapoor, a South Park Commons fellow who earlier worked in healthcare technology, co-founded Bharat Semi in late 2021 with Vinayak Dalmia (pictured above, left), the startup’s managing director, who previously worked at McKinsey and in private equity. Its chief technology officer, Boyd Fowler, previously held the same role at image-sensor maker OmniVision. Bharat Semi is targeting smart homes, industrial automation, surveillance, and aerospace. Without disclosing specifics, Kapoor pointed to air conditioners that could detect when a room is empty and adjust automatically and drones that could process visual information — even with the absence of more expensive computing hardware elsewhere in the system. The startup’s first-generation sensors are already in prototyping, while its second-generation sensors, which will incorporate more advanced AI capabilities, are expected to reach the prototype stage by mid-2027, Kapoor said. Moreover, the startup plans to get those newer sensors into customers’ hands by the end of 2027. The all-equity seed round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons, and Indus Bridge Ventures, with participation from Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels, and individual investors. Bharat Semi, Kapoor said, plans to use the funding to expand its engineering team, complete product development, and bring its sensors to market. Bharat Semi has about 75 employees across India and the U.S., including 10 to 12 in its American operations, which span engineering and business development in Santa Clara. The startup plans to increase its U.S. headcount to around 20 by mid-2027, Kapoor said. It has also begun hiring engineers in Europe. “It’s a story of can we build a global technology company out of India,” Kapoor said. In 2024, Bharat Semi announced plans for a semiconductor fabrication project in India involving a technology partnership with the U.S. Space Force. The initiative, Kapoor said, remains in development and the startup is working to identify domestic partners that would build and operate the facility. The project is separate from Bharat Semi’s image-sensor business, Kapoor added. The startup plans to remain fabless, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on semiconductor design and software. The new funding will not be used to finance the proposed fabrication facility. articles.title: Vulcan rocket fails during launch, dealing major blow to SpaceX competitors
articles.description: This was the first total mission failure in United Launch Alliance's 20-year history.
articles.content: United Launch Alliance's Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry. The Vulcan rocket is on contract to launch roughly half of the US military's national security space missions in the next few years, and Sunday's mission was the first of 38 Vulcan launches booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX's Starlink. Sunday's failure is expected to ground the rocket for an indefinite period of time. Vulcan is no stranger to close calls, having overcome failures with its strap-on solid rocket boosters on two of its four previous flights. In each case, the rocket corrected for those problems and continued into orbit to deploy its payloads. The incidents triggered monthslong reviews and investigations before ULA could resume Vulcan flights.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Israel kills a top Hamas commander as Jordan sentences 3 in church attack, and other Mideast news
articles.description: Israel kills a top Hamas commander as Jordan sentences 3 in church attack, and other Mideast news AP News Israel kills senior Hamas commander in Gaza two months after killing his predecessor as ceasefire stagnates CNN Israeli military says it struck senior member of Hamas military wing CNA Israel kills Hamas commander in strike on Gaza camp, officials say BBC Daily Briefing Nov. 16 – IDF strikes head of Hamas’s Rafah
articles.content: Israeli forces killed a top commander of the militant Hamas group in an overnight airstrike on southern Gaza, Israel said Sunday. In Jordan, three men were sentenced to death for a deadly shooting last month at a Greek Orthodox Church. In Yemen, the Houthis said they freed around 600 detainees captured in the latest escalation of fighting, even as they consolidated their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Sunday. Read our full coverage here. Israel said it killed a top Hamas commander in an airstrike on southern Gaza just after midnight. A Hamas statement confirmed the killing of Samir Mahmoud Hassan Abu Younis and said a funeral would be held for him later Sunday. The Israeli military said Abu Younis had been directing plans “to advance and carry out terror attacks.” Two months earlier, an Israeli strike killed his predecessor. The military said it targeted other Hamas militants in Sunday’s strike but provided no details. Jordan’s State Security Court on Sunday sentenced three men to death for a deadly shooting at a Greek Orthodox Church last month, state-run Al Mamlaka TV said. The men were charged with “carrying out terrorist acts.” The Oct. 23 attack was one of the deadliest on Jordan’s Christian minority in decades, with nine people killed and dozens wounded. The attackers targeted mourners attending a funeral at St. George’s Church in Hamoud, a village south of the capital, Amman. The three defendants — two brothers and their brother-in-law — were arrested three days after the attack following a shootout with security forces. Jordanian authorities described the men as followers of an extremist ideology but said they were not affiliated with an organized group. The Iran-backed Houthis on Sunday freed some 600 detainees captured in the latest escalation of fighting, the largest unilateral release of detainees in the country’s 12-year civil war, said Abdul-Qader al-Murtaza, a Houthi official on prisoners’ affairs. Also Sunday, a group allied with the Saudi-backed Yemeni government said its fighters pulled out from areas along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait amid relentless attacks by the Houthis. The Southern Armed Forces said they would now focus on securing Yemen’s southern city of Aden, held by the internationally recognized government, as well as trying to break the Houthi siege of the crucial city of Taiz. The move has allowed the rebels to consolidate their grip on the strait, in a setback to the Saudi-backed efforts to dislodge them from the strategic coastal territories on the Red Sea. In Aden, an Associated Press journalist heard sounds of explosions Sunday evening. Local media reported that the Houthis fired two ballistic missiles on the district of Buraiqeh on Aden’s western coast. Clashes were reported between the Houthis and government forces in an area in Yemen’s southwestern province of Lahj, which has key supply routes close to the Bab el-Mandeb strait. The Houthis said they fired ballistic missiles on government forces’ positions in the Kharaz area, which is home to a refugee camp sheltering thousands of African refugees. The U.N. refugee agency warned Sunday that the clashes hindered its efforts to offer protection and aid to about 9,600 refugees. Iran’s paramilitary Revolutionary Guard clashed with members of the Kurdish Iranian dissident group Kurdistan Free Life Party, or PJAK, near Iran’s border with Iraq, both groups said in statements Sunday. The IRGC said it “destroyed” a group of PJAK fighters “that intended to enter the territory of the Islamic Republic of Iran and carry out terrorist actions” and seized “a quantity of weapons, equipment and explosive materials.” The IRGC statement did not specify when the clash took place, but PJAK said that one of its members was killed Wednesday after a group of fighters were “ambushed” by IRGC forces in Sardasht, in western Iran. PJAK and other Kurdish Iranian dissident groups have bases in northern Iraq that have been frequently targeted by Iran since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28. In the early days of the war, some of the Kurdish groups said they planned to launch an incursion into Iran with U.S. support, but the plan was later abandoned. Israel’s military said it apprehended a stringer for Agence France-Presse in the occupied West Bank very early on Sunday on suspicion of “terror ties,” adding that he was transferred to the security forces for more questioning. The French news agency called for Israel to provide evidence in the detention of Mohammad Ateeq, a video journalist who has contributed to AFP for three years. His wife said that Israeli forces blindfolded him and took him away from his home in a town near Jenin, according to AFP. Iran’s Revolutionary Guard claimed early on Sunday that it struck a radar system at an American helicopter base in Bahrain, the state-run IRNA news agency reported. The U.S. military’s Central Command, which oversees American forces in the Middle East, did not immediately comment. On Friday, CENTCOM had said it intercepted two Iranian drones headed toward Bahrain and denied an Iranian claim at the time that it had struck a U.S. early-warning radar system there. Bahrain’s military said Sunday its air defense systems intercepted a number of Iranian projectiles before they reached their targets. This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge. This story was corrected earlier to say that the shooting in Jordan took place in the village of Hamoud in the Karak governorate, not in the city of Karak.

A step toward defining the Standard Model on a lattice
articles.description: Explore a candidate nonperturbative lattice definition of the Standard Model and how GPT-6 Astra helped turn the idea into a detailed proof.
articles.content: In the first guest post on our science blog, physicist Nathaniel Craig, a visiting scientist at OpenAI, describes how he worked with GPT‑6 Astra on a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model. Craig leads the particle theory group at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and is a permanent member of its Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics. The Standard Model of particle physics is an extraordinarily successful theory of nature, describing the known elementary particles and three of the four fundamental forces—the strong force, the weak force, and electromagnetism. The success of the theory rests on outstanding agreement between theoretical calculations and experiments across eighteen orders of magnitude, from the low energies of hydrogen’s 21-centimeter radio emission to the high energies of collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. And yet for all of its successes over the more than fifty years of its existence, a foundational problem remains: how to give the full theory a nonperturbative definition, one that does not rely on treating its interactions as small corrections. In an October preprint(opens in a new window) prepared with the aid of GPT‑6 Astra, I proposed a candidate definition on a lattice—a grid representing spacetime. I had a strategy for tackling this problem, but had not been able to prove that it worked in all the cases it needed to cover. Astra helped turn that strategy into a construction and took the lead in developing the detailed proof. To explain what we did, it helps to start with what is missing from our existing description of the Standard Model. What does it mean to say that we lack a definition of the Standard Model? Quantum mechanics and special relativity tell us how the particles and forces of the Standard Model interact. Unfortunately, we don’t yet know how to make complete predictions based directly on these interactions. Instead, we often start by imagining that the interactions are turned off, so that electrons would no longer repel each other. We can solve that problem exactly, then put the interactions back in as a series of small corrections. When the corrections get progressively smaller, a few terms can give a remarkably precise answer—for example, it has allowed physicists to predict the strength of the electron’s magnetism to within a few parts in a trillion. This approach is known as perturbation theory. However, much of the richness of the Standard Model lies outside the realm of perturbation theory. Take the mass of the proton: the proton is made up of three quarks, but its mass comes primarily from the motion and interactions of the quarks and the strong force-carrying gluons inside it. If you turn off the strong force, the proton falls apart entirely, so perturbation theory is not a useful guide to understanding the size of the proton’s mass. More powerful methods are needed to access information about the theory nonperturbatively, where the interactions are present from the start and not treated as small corrections. For the full Standard Model in continuous spacetime, we don’t have a nonperturbative definition, or even an understanding of whether the interacting theory is mathematically well defined. A promising alternative is to discretize spacetime into a grid of points, known as a lattice. The spacing of the grid defines the shortest distance our theory can resolve, and studying a finite grid allows us to give a rigorous nonperturbative definition of the theory at a given spacing. It also enables us to put the theory on a computer, where we can calculate its predictions directly without resorting to perturbation theory. This approach, known as lattice field theory, has led to remarkable progress in our understanding of the strong force over the last few decades, including a quantitative understanding of the mass of the proton from first principles. If lattice field theory has been so successful for the strong force, why haven’t we extended it to a nonperturbative lattice definition of the entire Standard Model? Here a crucial difference stands in the way: the Standard Model is an example of what is known as a chiral theory. A chiral theory is one that looks different under reflection in space. Think of gloves in a mirror: the mirror image of a left-handed glove is a right-handed glove. If you have one of each kind, the mirror image does as well, so your collection of gloves looks the same under reflection in space. But if you only have a left-handed glove, the right-handed glove in the mirror is different. This notion of handedness extends to many of the fundamental particles in the Standard Model, known as fermions, including quarks and electrons. Most forces in the Standard Model are not chiral: the strong force and electromagnetism, for example, treat left-handed and right-handed fermions in the same way. Such theories can be put on a lattice more readily. But the third fundamental force of the Standard Model, the weak force, lacks this reflection symmetry. It treats left- and right-handed fermions differently, and so does not look the same under mirror reflections that exchange left and right. This treating of different-handed particles differently is what makes the Standard Model a chiral theory. And it turns out that putting chiral theories on a lattice is profoundly challenging. If we try to put a left-handed fermion on the lattice, the most natural rules give you a right-handed partner you never asked for. This is a surprising outcome, which we’ll unpack momentarily. Whatever the reason, this means a straightforward lattice formulation of the Standard Model gives the wrong particle content for the weak force. Doubling is one reason a complete nonperturbative definition of the Standard Model has been missing since the theory took shape. To understand doubling, consider an analogy with light. Light has two polarizations, which describe the orientation of the electric field as the light moves through space. (This is familiar if you wear polarized sunglasses, which block the horizontally-polarized light that reflects off water or roads while letting through vertically-polarized light.) Although polarized sunglasses pick out a basis of horizontal and vertical polarizations, for our analogy it will be more useful to pick a basis where these two polarizations are left-circular and right-circular, meaning that the electric field is rotating either clockwise or counterclockwise around the direction of motion. As we’ve said, electromagnetism is reflection-symmetric, so its actual laws are the same for both left-circular and right-circular polarizations. (For the technically inclined, left and right refer to chirality when we talk about fermions. In our analogy with light, they refer to the photon’s helicity, which tells us whether its spin points along or against its direction of travel.) But imagine you wanted to emulate a world with only left-circular light, akin to the way the weak interactions single out left-handed fermions. To study this in the lab, you could put a laser producing left-circular light into a box with a mirror at either end. The light could build up as it bounced back and forth, allowing you to study it carefully—kind of like putting the Standard Model on a lattice. In each case you are bounding the accessible length scales of the theory to gain control—the lattice bounds the shortest accessible distances, while the box bounds the longest distances. If you built the box using ordinary mirrors (like putting a chiral theory on the lattice in the most straightforward way), you’d be in for a surprise: the left-circular light coming out of the laser becomes right-circular when it bounces off the mirror at the other end, so now the box contains both polarizations of light. This occurs because the mirror reverses the direction of the light without changing how the electric field is rotating (as seen from the same end of the box), which flips the polarization. This is a bit like the appearance of doublers when you put a left-handed fermion on the lattice. You supplied only left-handed light, and the box supplied the other hand. There is a clever fix. You can make a chiral mirror using special films whose molecules line up in layers. The alignment turns a little from one layer to the next, tracing a spiral down into the film. For light whose wavelength and handedness match the spiral, the small reflections from different layers reinforce one another, flipping the rotation of the electric field in the light that bounces back. The film sends left-handed light back left-handed and lets right-handed light pass through. Such chiral mirrors have been around for more than a decade, and the phenomenon even occurs in nature: some scarab beetles have a similar spiral in their shiny shells. If you constructed your box using chiral mirrors, then the light traveling in both directions would be left-circular. A similar trick works on the lattice: decades ago, Paul Ginsparg and Nobel laureate Ken Wilson1 worked out the lattice rules analogous to the requirement that chiral mirrors reverse the rotation of the electric field upon reflection. Rajamani Narayanan and Herbert Neuberger2 built the analog of the chiral mirrors by finding the necessary definition of fundamental particles on the lattice, known as overlap fermions. Finally, Martin Lüscher3 showed how to tell the difference between left-handed and right-handed overlap fermions on the lattice, while Yoshio Kikukawa4 and collaborators explored how this might be used to describe weak interactions in the Standard Model. However, one piece was still missing. To identify that piece, let’s come back to our box with chiral mirrors. The circular polarization of light tells us which way the electric field turns as light propagates, but there’s another important property of the light in our experiment: the optical phase. Imagine water waves rolling past the pilings of a dock, and watch the water rise and fall at one piling. The wave’s phase is the stage of that rise and fall you catch it in when you look, perhaps just past its highest point and on its way down. For our circularly polarized light, the optical phase tracks the same kind of cycle at a fixed spot in the beam, with the electric field pointing up at the “crest” and down at the “trough.” The relative phase of two waves determines how much they add or cancel at the same point. At one piling of a dock, two waves arriving in phase lift the water higher as their crests meet, while a crest arriving with a trough can leave the water close to its usual level. Similarly, light with the same phase in the same place builds up, while light with different phases can cancel out. In our box with chiral mirrors, left-circular light is now bouncing back and forth inside the box. After a lap, the returning light meets fresh light from the laser going in the same direction. If their electric fields are in step, they reinforce and the light builds up inside the box. If the fields are half a cycle apart, they point in opposite directions and the returning light cancels some of the fresh light. To build up a strong beam, we want the phase of each return to arrive in step with the source. To get the phase right, we can rotate one chiral mirror relative to the other. Imagine a mark at twelve o’clock on the rim, and spin the mirror about the beam as though the beam were its axle. Moving the mark to three o’clock turns every layer of the film by a quarter turn and shifts the phase of the reflected light by half a cycle. We can set the angle to make up for the phase accumulated on the rest of the trip. Once the returning light arrives in step with the laser, we have a splendid laboratory for studying purely left-handed light. Imagine changing the force fields until they return to where they started. articles.title: Is bad news for Jensen Huang also bad news for the AI industry?
articles.description: "Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia."
articles.content: We didn’t see this coming. Or at least, I didn’t — a week ago, when I wrote about Nvidia’s board opening an investigation into then-CEO Jensen Huang, I assumed his job was safe. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Rebecca Bellan, Tim De Chant, and I discussed how Huang’s ouster went down and what it means for the larger AI economy. While Tim said he saw it coming (albeit not this quickly), Rebecca said, “I didn’t think it was going to happen at all.” “Jensen is Nvidia, right?” she added. “And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia.” Similarly, I marveled at how quickly Huang’s support seemed to crumble, with more scandals seeming to emerge every day. (At the same time, there are many who’d still like to see him return.) And we also took a moment to wonder what will happen to Nvidia’s investments in the larger AI ecosystem. Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity; you can listen to the whole episode here. Tim De Chant: I figured this was coming. I didn’t think it would happen this quickly. I thought there would be at least a few days. Rebecca Bellan: I didn’t think it was going to happen at all. I mean, Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia. And we’ve got nothing but the last few years of data to show us that billionaires can do whatever the hell they want. So it was surprising to me — it almost restored my faith in humanity, that he resigned. But someone said to me, “If this were Elon, nothing would happen.” He would not be resigning. Nothing would be going down Anthony Ha: Which is interesting, because I would have said, as of a week ago, or even just a few days ago, that Jensen is in the same category as Elon. I mean, no one is quite as special as Elon is, but it’s a big, incredibly successful company. Like you said — in a lot of ways, the entire AI economy is built on top of Nvidia. And for most people, Jensen Huang is Nvidia. He’s the biggest shareholder. He has family members who work at the company, and probably most importantly, there was no succession plan in place. So this was not something that they were prepared for at all. Rebecca: I think we should actually take a step back, because we just launched into this conversation assuming — rightly so — that our listeners will know what the heck we’re talking about. But for those who somehow don’t, Jensen resigned on Thursday, after it came out he was having an affair with a former executive at an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, who’s alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. And then there was another reported affair with an Nvidia executive. So he’s resigned. Nvidia CFO Collette Kress is jumping in as the interim CEO. She’s a longtime board member. I think it’s always interesting when a CFO steps in to be a CEO. It just means we’re going to manage expenses right now, like that’s the key. Anthony: I think a big part of the message is: This is not necessarily someone you should expect to be in this role for the long term. No disrespect to her, but it feels like a caretaker appointment while they figure things out. Just to get into that backstory a little bit more, what has been really remarkable to me has been this sense that a lot of what ultimately brought Huang down, [that] stuff was at least known in intelligence circles for a while. Apparently, this report that [raises] questions, concerns about his relationship with Alice Huang is something that was circulating a year ago, or close to a year ago. And then suddenly, everything really accelerated, Starting over the weekend, with Jensen Huang admitting to having an affair, the board saying it was investigating, but that it still had a lot of faith in him. And then this week, this other affair being reported on, and it just felt like there was all this bad news coming fairly quickly. But also, it wasn’t this thing that no one had known before. I guess a lot of the general public hadn’t known. So it’s this combined feeling of, “Wow, the ground kind of shifted so quickly under him,” even though the worst stuff, the possibility that somehow national security might have been threatened, is something that actually has been known by the government for nearly a year, if not more. Rebecca: That’s exactly right. Trump was given some warnings about Huang’s affair with someone who has ties to Chinese intelligence, potentially, and it seemed like he didn’t really mind. I think what’s important here, though, is to note that Jensen Huang has been an advocate for loosening chip exports to China. And so this is where the crux of it is. Can anyone trust him as the CEO of this company when he’s advocating for loosening chip exports to China? Which a lot of people believe is a national security issue, because that means it will give Chinese AI companies access to our powerful chips, which will help them improve their AI, which could threaten America. I mean, there’s two sides of this coin. And I think, honestly, that Jensen does not need a woman to tell him that — he just wants to sell more chips, and to anybody and everybody, and whether or not that’s good for national security or not, I think is honestly secondary to him. Tim: I completely agree. I think the big turning point seems to happen on November 9 — so that would have been earlier this week, Monday, when the Bloomberg report came out and suggested that Nvidia’s head attorney had some role in inquiring about the Department of Commerce’s investigation into Alice Huang. Things seem to have accelerated in the last few days following that. And I don’t know what role exactly that report played in it, but it seems to be maybe there was a shift within government or within the board, a kind of a daunting realization of the extent to which this had spread just beyond Jensen and some affair. Anthony: There’s also just the question of: What does this mean for Nvidia? What does this mean for the broader AI industry? And one of the reasons those two things are very tightly connected is not just Nvidia chips themselves, but also the fact that under Jensen Huang, the company has invested very, very heavily in a number of AI startups. People talk about the idea of an AI circular economy, and I think Nvidia has been one of the biggest players in that, in terms of both funding a lot of things, [but] also, obviously, providing the infrastructure for a lot of AI projects. So if Nvidia is going into this stage of lockdown, circle the wagons — even if it just means a small pullback, that could have really dramatic repercussions. Rebecca: Yeah, that’s what I want to know: What happens to the Bank of Nvidia without Jensen? Is he the one leading this? Just to throw some numbers at you, Nvidia apparently accounts for roughly 80% of the AI GPU market. It reported $99 billion in investments and another $25 billion in commitments, plus $36 billion dollars in cloud service commitments. A lot of those include investments into CoreWeave, Nebius, OpenAI, Anthropic, major data center projects. They’ve got their fingers in literally everybody’s pie. Roseville man in custody after parents shot to death
articles.content: A 31-year-old man is being held in custody after his parents were found shot to death in their Roseville home early Sunday, according to police and neighbors. Residents on the 30000 block of Bluehill Street, near 13 Mile and Calahan roads, say they were awakened about 4:30 a.m. to the suspect screaming on their front lawns. “I didn’t know who it was, but it scared the hell out of me,” said one neighbor, who asked not to be identified. “I thought it was a random attack. He was yelling in what sounded to be a very different language than American.” According to the Roseville Police Department, officers responded to a report of a disorderly person about 5 a.m. at a residence on Bluehill Street. One person was detained when officers noticed a shattered door at a nearby residence, said Roseville Police Chief Scott Burley. “While checking the home, they located two deceased individuals,” police said in a new release. The suspected shooter remains in police custody. He was transported to an area hospital for treatment of unknown medical condition. Nearby homeowners said the parents live on Bluehill with their adult son. A second son was not at home at the time of the shooting, they said. Neighbors said Sunday’s incident was surprising since the suspected shooter had been working for the past few weeks on a brick arrangement outside the house. The family was quiet and kept to themselves, according to neighbors. “The guy seemed to be severely bipolar because he was on my front lawn, just scream for 45 minutes straight before the police got here,” one neighbor told the Macomb Daily. “I could just hear screaming that he’s got a bomb and he’s going to kill them all.” Investigators have not identified the two shooting victims. The Roseville Police Department’s Criminal Investigation Division is leading the probe. Police said based on the information available, the department believes there is no ongoing threat to the public, Burley said. The department will provide updates as the investigation continues. It was the second straight weekend where a shooting had taken place in Roseville. A man was found shot in the back Saturday Nov. 7 in the parking lot of an industrial business on Common Road, west of Groesbeck Highway. Police have not made an arrest in that incident. Anyone with information about Sunday’s shooting is asked to contact the Roseville Police Department’s Criminal Investigation Division at 586-447-4507.

articles.description: 32 Americans named as Rhodes scholars have variety of interests, from space junk to art history AP News Two Penn fourth-years named 2027 Rhodes Scholars Penn Today Two young people from the Philly area awarded 2027 Rhodes scholarships Inquirer.com The 2027 Class Of U.S. Rhodes Scholars Has Been Announced Forbes
articles.content: WASHINGTON (AP) — A college senior who wants to clean up debris pollution in Earth’s orbit and a student who has researched AI use in healthcare are among the 32 Americans named as 2027 Rhodes scholars. The winners, who were announced on Saturday, have a variety of interests, from bioelectronics to water scarcity to art history. They were chosen from 238 finalists who emerged from more than 1,000 candidates who received formal endorsements from their colleges and universities for the honor. The students will attend the University of Oxford in England as part of the Rhodes scholar program, which awards more than 100 scholarships worldwide each year for students to pursue two to three years of graduate studies. Two students are the first-ever Rhodes scholars from their schools — Prairie View A&M University in Texas and The Citadel — The Military College of South Carolina. Harvard University led the way with four 2027 Rhodes scholars, followed by Yale and Princeton with three each. Evan Garrison, of Webb City, Missouri, a senior at Mississippi State University majoring in aerospace engineering and mathematics. His research includes designing ways to detect objects in space, with an interest in cleaning up orbital debris known as “space junk.” He plans to study mathematical modeling, scientific computing and global governance and diplomacy at Oxford. Asuka Koda, of New York City, a senior at Yale University majoring in mathematics and philosophy. She has researched AI adoption in healthcare and has been a health and science writer for CNN. She plans to study social science of the internet and international health and tropical medicine at Oxford. Michael Bueker, from Wellesley, Massachusetts, a senior at Dartmouth College majoring in biomedical engineering. His research has focused on biodegradable, implantable neural stimulators and other ultrathin bioelectronic devices. He also grows giant pumpkins. At Oxford, he intends to study engineering science. Elizabeth Koenck, of Aurora, Colorado, a senior at Georgetown University majoring in foreign service. Her research has examined water scarcity problems across the Middle East, North Africa and the Colorado River Basin. She plans to pursue degrees in migration studies and water science, policy and management at Oxford. Sabrina Soriano, of Azusa, California, a senior at Yale University majoring in art history. Her research includes 19th-century French painting, with a focus on the relationship between art, religion and cultural identity. She plans to study history of art and visual culture and visual, material and museum anthropology at Oxford. Named after British imperialist and benefactor Cecil John Rhodes, the scholarships were established at Oxford in 1903. The program has more than 8,000 alumni, many of whom have pursued careers in government, education, the arts and social justice.

articles.content: MUNICH (AP) —Detroit Lions edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson has a season-ending right knee injury, according to a person familiar with the situation. The person spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity Sunday night because Hutchinson’s condition had not been announced. Hutchinson hurt his knee while celebrating a sack of New England’s Drake Maye in the first quarter of Detroit’s 35-10 win in Munich. Lions coach Dan Campbell told reporters more would be known about Hutchinson’s injury when the team returned to the United States. “Any time you lose a player like that and you don’t know the entirety of it … it hurts a little bit,” Campbell said. Earlier on Sunday, the Ringer’s Tom Pelissero reported that the injury is significant: “Imaging in Munich confirmed the injury to Hutchinson, whose right knee buckled as he celebrated a sack against the Patriots. He’s out for the season.” Hutchinson leaped in the air but went straight to the ground after landing. He immediately grabbed his right knee. He stayed down and eventually was able to walk to the blue tent for evaluation. He then walked gingerly to the locker room and didn’t return to the game. Hutchinson had sacked Maye on third down at the Detroit 15-yard line on New England’s first drive. Andy Borregales then kicked a 33-yard field goal. Detroit hosts Tampa Bay (3-6) on Sunday. The Lions (7-2) have won five straight games to surge into a first-place tie in the NFC North with Minnesota and Chicago. Green Bay is in last place in the stout division with a 6-4 record. Detroit, though, has lost two of its best players during the winning streak. All-Pro linebacker Jack Campbell is on injured reserve with a neck injury after a tackle left him motionless on the turf and sent him to the hospital. Hutchinson had six sacks in nine games this season, giving him 49 career sacks since Detroit drafted the former Michigan star with the No. 2 pick in 2022. He finished second in Defensive Rookie of the Year voting with 9 1/2 sacks and had 11 1/2 sacks in his second season. Five games into the 2024 season, he had 7 1/2 sacks before breaking his left leg in two places. After having surgery, he bounced back in 2025 with a career-high 14 1/2 sacks to finish second in Comeback Player of the Year voting and was a second-team AP All-Pro. Early last season, he signed a four-year, $180 million deal that includes $141 million in guarantees and keeps him under contract through the 2030 season. articles.content: A public hearing on a secretive large-scale project that many suspect could be a data center in Lenox Township could be jeopardized by litigation filed by a nearby industrial business. Shoreline Steel Supply and its owners, Mark and Matthew Phillips, say a legal advertisement for the public hearing scheduled for Monday, Nov. 16, contains several errors or omissions in it. They filed an emergency motion asking a Macomb County Circuit Court judge to issue a temporary restraining order to block the hearing. “This request for injunctive relief is not seeking this Court’s opinion as to whether (Lenox Township) should permit a data center,” attorney Steven Cohen wrote in a complaint. “It is seeking this Court’s ruling as to whether the Township can advance the rezoning without complying with mandatory legal requirements.” A hearing on the matter is scheduled for 8:20 a.m. Monday, Nov. 16, before Circuit Judge Michael E. Servitto. That’s roughly 10 hours before the Lenox Township Planning Commission public hearing. A company known as Lenox & Chesterfield Economic Development Alliance, LLC, is asking Lenox Township officials to rezone about 1,400 acres of land for a 2-million-square-foot development. Although it’s not mentioned in other paperwork, attorneys for the company previously informed township officials that they were working to build a data center campus on land near Interstate 94. Named as defendants in the lawsuit are Lenox Township and its planning commission, Township Supervisor Anthony Reeder Jr., Spartan Real Estate Group, Paul Reschke, Joseph Rosseel, Rosseel Properties, and Lenox & Chesterfield Economic Development Alliance. Shoreline is a supplier of cold-formed steel sheet piling and marine/civil engineering products, according to its website. According to the lawsuit, the Phillips brothers own approximately 104 acres of agricultural land consisting of five separate parcels along Gratiot Avenue and several land-locked parcels. The properties connect on three sides with the property that is proposed for rezoning and that has been the subject of an attempt to secure land for the development of a data center, attorneys for the Phillips said in their complaint. The property is presently zoned agricultural and has direct access to a tie in to municipal water. Attorneys for Shoreline Steel list the following alleged defects on the notice for Monday’s public hearing: Attorney Robert Kirk said the Phillips family opposes the data center plan. The lawsuit states the Phillips have been approached by some of the defendants to grant an option to purchase the properties for purposes of inclusion in a rezoning and/or redistricting effort to market the property for a data center, the lawsuit states. They have not authorized Lenox and Chesterfield Economic Development Alliance LLC or anyone else to petition the property for rezoning. The request seeks to rezone 49 properties covering 1,402 acres, located roughly between New Haven, I-94, 29 Mile Road and 26 Mile Road. It includes the entire Oak Ridge Golf Course. The Lenox Township Planning Commission will conduct a special meeting to hold the public hearing at 6:30 p.m. Monday, Nov. 16. The meeting will be held at the township municipal offices, 63775 Gratiot Ave. Lenox.

articles.title: Climate progressives won the midterms without saying ‘climate’
articles.description: “This story was originally published by Grist. Sign up for Grist’s weekly newsletter here.” On October 20, the two candidates running to represent Michigan in the U.S. Senate, Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers, took questions for an hour at the Detroit Economic Club. El-Sayed, the Democrat who had previously run for governor, made a name […]
articles.content: From left: Will Lawrence, Claire Valdez, Abdul El-Sayed, and Darializa Avila Chevalier. Grist / Getty Images“This story was originally published by Grist. Sign up for Grist’s weekly newsletter here.” On October 20, the two candidates running to represent Michigan in the U.S. Senate, Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers, took questions for an hour at the Detroit Economic Club. El-Sayed, the Democrat who had previously run for governor, made a name for himself years ago by connecting public health to the climate crisis. He published a fierce defense of the Green New Deal at the time, touting its economic, health, and planetary benefits. But last month at the Detroit Economic Club, El-Sayed didn’t mention the Green New Deal at all. Instead, the only mentions of such a plan came from his opponent, who used it as an attack on El-Sayed and the Democratic party as a whole. “We need to make sure we don’t have the largest tax increase in the history of the country,” Rogers said, “which is, that’s what the other team is talking about doing.” A vote for El-Sayed would ring in an era of “big government, government control, more rules, more regulation, another Green New Deal,” Rogers continued. It’s become a common refrain since President Donald Trump’s effort to rebrand the climate movement’s push for widescale public investment in renewable energy as a “Green New Scam.” Two weeks later, El-Sayed handily won the race. Even though many of the newly elected Democrats did not talk about the Green New Deal by name, the think tank Climate and Community Institute describes El-Sayed as belonging to a new class of green economic populists who are running for public office (and winning) by connecting the need for climate action to soaring utility bills and the hoarding of wealth by a handful of individuals and companies. El-Sayed “clearly gets it,” said Patrick Bigger, research director at Climate and Community Institute, or CCI. The senator-elect’s platform, which proposes stricter regulations on data centers and energy companies, is “really exciting,” he said. These are promising climate agenda items — even if Democrats don’t explicitly call them that. For example, voters may oppose data centers in their backyard for any number of reasons, but some number of them are required for our digitalized reality and progressives now have an opportunity to take the companies behind them to task and get them to commit to reducing their strain on the local environment. Likewise, where voters came out in support of lowering utility bills, electeds now can talk further about investing in cheaper renewable energy systems like solar and wind power. Bigger led a recent analysis that scored candidates in this year’s primary and midterm elections based on three questions: Is the candidate pushing for renewable energy or other climate actions? Do they name the rising cost of living as a voter issue, and have a plan to lower those costs? Do they articulate a populist vision by blaming wealthy corporations and powerful individuals for both the climate and affordability crises? CCI argues that candidates like El-Sayed who check all three boxes are the climate champions of the moment. Other progressives named in the report include Will Lawrence, a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, the climate group that first sounded the alarm for a Green New Deal in 2018. Lawrence, who will represent Michigan’s 7th District in the next Congress, points to his history of climate organizing on his website: “I will be among the most knowledgeable and dedicated members of Congress on water, climate and energy policy,” he writes. “I will fight for investment to secure the climate we depend on, adapt to the changes we can’t prevent, and finally drive our electric bills down.” These “new folks headed to the House and the Senate who are really on board with a robust transformative approach to climate,” said Bigger, represent “a major shift.” But not all climate progressives heading to Washington next year are so allergic to calling it the Green New Deal: Representatives-elect Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York City name it specifically on their campaign websites and in the press. Still, this new wave of climate leaders may feel it’s time for the decarbonization agenda to get a refresh; Valdez and Avila Chevalier’s websites also include mentions of “a livable planet for all” and “a livable world for everyone,” respectively. In part, this diversity of messaging tactics reflects the fractured nature of the climate movement since Trump retook office with a checklist of Biden-era environmental regulations to roll back. If progressive Democrats’ messaging on climate has shifted, said Aru Shiney-Ajay, executive director of the Sunrise Movement, it’s because the terrain they’re fighting in has changed, too. “I think, as the climate crisis gets worse and worse, it’s becoming increasingly clear that the strategy, policy-wise, needs to be incorporating climate change into every single aspect of what we’re doing,” she said. In other words, climate policy should not be framed as a separate issue from the economy, infrastructure improvements, or foreign policy. “It should be the defining framework within which we have to think about how we run our society,” said Shiney-Ajay. In 2018, the Sunrise Movement burst onto the national stage by protesting outside House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi’s office — with the Green New Deal as their top priority. Just seven years later, members of the Sunrise Movement voted to reorganize around the priority of fighting authoritarianism and, in particular, the second Trump administration. Shiney-Ajay acknowledged that the climate movement has suffered in recent years. But that doesn’t mean that the public has become disengaged from the climate crisis. In fact, voters across the political spectrum are more attuned to it than ever. “People are actually really hungry for something to do about climate change,” said Shiney-Ajay. “I think we will actually see a lot of momentum around stopping the climate crisis. And I certainly hope to build a movement that makes that possible.” Wherever climate progressives or so-called “green economic populists,” are in office, the CCI report says, now is the time to govern. (It’s worth noting that a petition launched this week asking Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who famously joined Sunrise members in the protest outside of Pelosi’s office, to run in the 2028 presidential race.) It will, of course, take more than the next two years, or the next presidential term, to solve the climate crisis. This article originally appeared in Grist at https://grist.org/elections/climate-progressives-won-the-midterms-without-saying-climate/. Grist is a nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to reporting on climate change.
