MOCAD celebrates two decades of making space for Detroit artists
articles.description: New exhibition brings together more than 80 local, national and international artists that have helped shape the Midtown institution since opening its doors in 2006.
articles.content: In Sterling Toles’ piece, “PT,” the Detroit artist explores the themes of recovering from trauma and reclaiming one’s humanity through an unlikely source–a potential transformer. The installation features a large electrical device illuminated by a ring light and surrounded by bright orange vinyl curtains. Toles said his art showcases objects that conduct energy, a metaphor for the pain and trauma that can weigh heavy on a person. “This PT (potential transformer) is basically taking a very large amount of electrical energy, distilling it down to where it can go to smaller places. I took that as a symbol of what we have the capacity to do as humans,” he told BridgeDetroit. “The hallmark of our humanity is that we have the ability to not merely transfer what we experience as humans, but transform what we experience through our own application and our action and our ability to engage with other people.” PT is one of the pieces featured in the Museum of Contemporary Art Detroit’s latest exhibition, “20 Years of MOCAD: A Practice of Multiplicity.” The show brings together more than 80 local, national and international artists that have helped shape the Midtown institution since opening its doors in 2006. Some of those names include Detroit legends Olayami Dabls, Tyree Guyton and Shirley Woodson, as well as newer artists like Bryce Detroit, LaKela Brown and Conrad Egyir. Detroit artist Sterling Toles’ installation “PT” explores reclaiming one’s humanity through an unlikely source–a potential transformer. Credit: Timothy Johnson MOCAD Co-Director and Artistic Director Jova Lynne said in a written statement that selecting the artists for the show was “an enormous curatorial undertaking,” and one of the biggest challenges was the physical limitations of the museum. “Our selection process considered artists who have played meaningful roles in MOCAD’s history, while also thinking about how their practices speak to one another across generations, disciplines, and cultural contexts,” she said. “We wanted to create a dialogue between artists and works that might not ordinarily be presented together, allowing new connections and interpretations to emerge.” Lynne added that the exhibition was a way to reflect on the museum’s history while thinking about its future. “What made this exhibition particularly meaningful was the responsibility of telling an institutional story that has never been singular or linear,” she said. “MOCAD has always been a space for experimentation, risk-taking, and dialogue, and we wanted the exhibition to reflect that complexity. Bringing together more than 80 artists across generations, disciplines, and moments in the museum’s history allowed us to celebrate the many voices that have contributed to its identity.” Spanning multiple disciplines like installations, paintings, sculptures and sound, 20 Years of MOCAD, unfolds in four parts that chronicles MOCAD’s evolution. Part I: Process Driven Purpose, highlights four experimental sound installations by contemporary artists and runs through March 21. Part II: Artist as Architect, explores artists as architects of space, experience and institutional possibility. Part III: Detroit as Material, examines how artists engage the city as an active material rather than a backdrop. Part IV: A Practice of Multiplicity, highlights artists whose work is rooted in community, care and lived experience. Parts 2, 3 and 4 run until April 4. Lynne said over the years, MOCAD has reimagined the idea of what a contemporary art museum can be. “Experimentation has always been central to our identity, not only in the work we present, but in how we think about the museum itself as a platform for artistic production, dialogue, and discovery,” she said. “One of MOCAD’s greatest strengths is its willingness to work across disciplines, bringing visual artists, musicians, performers, and cultural practitioners into conversation.” Process driven purpose This is the third time Toles has shown his work at MOCAD. The first was the museum’s 2021 group exhibition, “Dual Vision,” and his 2022 solo exhibition, “s(h)elves?” Initially a rapper and producer in Detroit’s music scene, the eastsider has added mixed media artist to his resume. Toles often uses repurposed objects for his pieces. When Lynne asked Toles to be a part of the latest exhibit it took him about a week to put together “PT” and another piece called, “s(h)elves, which features a picture of a man taped to an electrical device. Toles said he hopes that visitors that see the exhibit will leave with a sense of curiosity and an appreciation of beauty in their everyday lives. “We all want to experience something beautiful, but it’s hard to experience beauty when we have all these rules about perfection and about the way things should be,” he said. “It’s like, ‘How much more joy would we experience if we were able to see the beauty in everything that we encounter?’” Leith Campbell is another Detroit artist who enjoys finding objects to repurpose. As part of the artist collective Apetechnology, she makes post-industrial folk art with friend Chip Flynn that often mixes robotics with animatronics and sound. “We get together and collect junk from junkyards, finding old motors and pneumatics and hooking them up, so we can just do crazy things,” Campbell said. “Whip Salad” from artist collective Apetechnology features four machines with a kiosk where people can activate them and make the machines move. Credit: Timothy Johnson In 2012, Apetechnology created a large installation for MOCAD called “Vision in a Cornfield,” transforming older cars into works of art. For 20 Years of MOCAD, the group has the installation “Whip Salad” on display. The piece features four machines with a kiosk where people can activate and move them. “They have very interesting motions with chains and gears and linkages that attract the eye at the same time as providing their own sort of soundtrack,” Campbell said. Detroit artist Sydney G. James pays tribute to the city’s east side with her painting, “3-1-3 Kings of the East,” which depicts three artists James admires–Sheefy McFly, Tony Whlgn and Philip Simpson. Credit: Micah Walker, BridgeDetroit ‘Kings of the East’ Meanwhile, in Part III of the exhibition, acclaimed Detroit artist Sydney G. James pays tribute to the city’s east side with her painting, “3-1-3 Kings of the East.” The artwork, created for 313 Day earlier this year, depicts three artists James admires who also hail from the east side–Sheefy McFly, Tony Whlgn and Philip Simpson. “They’re three of my favorite brothers,” she said. “Tony brings healing vibes. He’s all about peace. We get more excitable energy from like Sheefy, whether it’s his work, his music, personality. And Phil brings his smile.” James said wants the three artists to feel familiar to people, like they’re a friend or family member. And she hopes that the piece is a gateway for people to look up McFly, Whlgn and Simpson’s works. “They’re not gonna ask permission,” James said. “They’re gonna figure it out, and they’re gonna create their own spaces, even if they’re not welcome into your space. That’s what I love most about them.” 20 Years of MOCAD: A Practice of Multiplicity Museum of Contemporary Art Detroit, 4454 Woodward Ave. Hours: Monday and Tuesday: Closed; Wednesday: 11 a.m.–5 p.m.; Thursday: 11 a.m.–8 p.m.; Friday: 11 a.m.–8 p.m.; Saturday: 11 a.m.–5 p.m.; Sunday: 11 a.m.–5 p.m. Phone: 313-832-6622

First embrace, lasting progress: newborn care reaches 6500 facilities across the Western Pacific
articles.content: The “first embrace” – immediate skin-to-skin contact – between a mother and her newborn can be life saving. Two new publications now show just how much Early Essential Newborn Care (EENC), developed by the World Health Organization (WHO), has helped transform newborn and maternal care across the WHO Western Pacific Region for over a decade. Since 2013, EENC has been introduced in approximately 6500 childbirth facilities across nine priority countries in the Region, while more than 42 500 health-care providers have received practical coaching. In 2023 assessments of EENC-implementing facilities, nearly 93% of full-term newborns received immediate skin-to-skin contact. Behind those figures is a profoundly human moment: a baby kept warm and calm on the mother's chest, a mother supported to initiate early and exclusive breastfeeding, and a family able to stay together at the start of life. Two new publications document how this change was achieved and what remains to be done. The WHO report Early Essential Newborn Care: Fourth Progress Report (2022-2023) charts regional milestones and remaining gaps, while the peer-reviewed article “Early essential newborn care: a decade of scaling up quality, life-saving interventions across East Asia and the Pacific (2013-2023)”, published in BMJ Global Health in June 2026, explains how countries achieved change at scale. EENC-implementing countries by year of implementation. PHL: Philippines; KHM: Cambodia; LAO: Lao People’s Democratic Republic; MNG: Mongolia; PNG: Papua New Guinea; SLB: Solomon Islands; CHN: China; VNM: Viet Nam; VUT: Vanuatu. Health facility staff coached in EENC, by country, 2010–2023. Source: estimated total number of health staff (hospitals and primary care facilities) coached in EENC from country programme reports, 2010–2023. Health facilities providing childbirth services that have introduced EENC (%), by country, 2015–2023. Source: proportion of estimated total number of facilities providing birth services (hospitals and primary care facilities) introducing EENC from country programme reports 2015–2023 The progress comes as newborn deaths remain an urgent challenge. In 2022, 100 585 newborns died in the Western Pacific Region – amounting to one newborn death every five minutes. Prematurity, complications during birth and infections remain among the leading causes. At the heart of EENC is the First Embrace: immediate and sustained skin-to-skin contact between mother and baby. Along with immediate drying, delayed cord clamping, and support for breastfeeding when the baby is ready, it helps protect newborns in the first minutes and hours when they are most vulnerable. EENC also includes resuscitation for babies who do not breathe at birth and Kangaroo Mother Care for preterm and low-birthweight babies. “What happens in the first moments after birth can shape a newborn’s chances of surviving and thriving. Simple, proven practices help keep a newborn warm and calm on the mother’s chest, and support a mother to begin breastfeeding,” said Dr Huong Tran, Director, Division of Health Promotion, Disease Prevention and Control, WHO Regional Office for the Western Pacific. “Countries have proven that these practices can transform care at scale when health workers have the support and systems to deliver them consistently.” The two publications show that more babies who might once have been separated from their mothers are now receiving care that keeps them together. By 2023, nearly three in four babies born by caesarean section in assessed facilities received immediate skin-to-skin contact. Among preterm and low-birthweight babies weighing 2000 grams or less, 56% received Kangaroo Mother Care, compared with 7% in 2015. Rather than relying on one-off classroom training, EENC uses small-group, on-the-job coaching right in the settings where health workers deliver care. Multidisciplinary hospital teams identify practical barriers – from how a delivery room is organized to whether operating-theatre procedures allow mother and baby to stay together – and use facility data to track whether changes are working. “Skin-to-skin contact may seem simple, but making it possible after every birth requires the preparation, commitment and dedication across the entire childbirth care team. EENC brought learning directly into the delivery room,” said Dr Delgermaa Vanya, Technical Officer, Maternal, Newborn and Child Health unit, WHO Regional Office for the Western Pacific. “Through hands-on coaching, teamwork and the use of facility data, health workers could identify obstacles and improve routine practices. That is how evidence-based guidance becomes everyday practice.” Of the nine implementing countries, five have already reached the regional target of introducing EENC in at least 80% of childbirth facilities, and three more are on track. The publications describe EENC as the largest regional collaboration globally to improve the quality of newborn care. The next challenge is to make these improvements universal and fully institutionalized. WHO is working with countries to build EENC into the education of future health workers, strengthen regular monitoring of care and support country-led quality improvement. The goal is straightforward: every mother supported, every health worker prepared and every newborn given a healthy start.

articles.title: NATO to skip a leaders’ summit in Albania next year as high-level meetings are scaled back
articles.content: BRUSSELS (AP) — NATO is scaling back its high-level meetings and will not hold a leaders’ summit in Albania next year as previously planned amid tension within the alliance over defense spending, Iran and the war in Ukraine. Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama said Thursday that “there is not yet a common position on when the summit will happen, for sure not in 2027.” He said that “in 2028, if it will be a summit, it will be in Tirana,” Albania’s capital. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte played down the issue. “We are flexible with NATO summits,” he told The Associated Press in an interview. “We have summits when we need them,” he said, and will hold the next one “when a necessity is there.” Until about a decade ago, NATO held summits every two years. It’s not just about gatherings between U.S. President Donald Trump and his counterparts. NATO defense ministers usually meet in October, but no talks took place last month, and none are planned for October 2027. Foreign ministers only have one scheduled meeting next year, instead of two, under what NATO describes as a “reorganization package.” U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have each skipped a NATO meeting or left before talks ended since they came to office. Hegseth has used defense ministerial gatherings to berate or cajole European allies and Canada. The planned summit in Albania highlights the alliance’s challenges. Albania was appointed next year’s host in 2025, but its name was removed from a July summit declaration. Some allies believe that Albania is not spending enough on defense and they were reluctant to reward the country with NATO’s big event. The government in Tirana is projected to spend 2.15% of its gross domestic product on defense this year. NATO’s target is for the 32 allies to spend 3.5% of GDP on core defense by 2035, and 1.5% on defense-related infrastructure. Albania is not the worst offender among the 32 member countries. Spain, Belgium and Slovenia are faring much worse. But hosting a summit itself has tremendous financial and political costs. The Netherlands required a year of preparation ahead of the 2025 meeting in The Hague, and a roughly $100 million investment. Officials said NATO would have needed to decide on Albania by October for it to have enough time to organize a summit next year. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who hosted this year’s gala in his sprawling palace complex in Ankara, refurbished a military airport for leaders to arrive at, and mobilized tens of thousands of security personnel — virtually shutting down parts of the capital. Non-essential public workers were given a week off. “There’s always a lot of security involved,” Rutte told AP. “It is a costly event to organize a meeting with 32 allies and then partner countries and the Indo-Pacific partners we have, like Japan and Korea, Australia, New Zealand.” Asked whether it was all worth it, Rutte said: “It is.” The summit in Turkey was also a political spectacle. It threatened to go off the rails even before Trump and his counterparts sat down to work. Trump revived old talk about taking control of Greenland, a self-governing part of NATO ally Denmark, striking at the heart of the reason that the organization was formed in 1949: mutual defense. He also demanded “loyalty,” accusing NATO of failing to back his war on Iran. Summits are usually a sober show of resolve and unity of purpose by the member countries to dissuade any adversary that might be tempted to test NATO. European allies suspect that Russia wants to do just that. In Ankara, Rutte led a “big reveal” defense industry splash to try to convince the American leader that allies are spending big. Besides the price tag, and the costs of keeping Trump on side, experts say that perhaps enough has been achieved for now. New spending goals and military capability targets have been set, and force planning was discussed in Ankara. “There’s a strong argument to be made that if there aren’t things that merit bringing 32 leaders together, well then maybe you don’t have the meeting,” said David Cattler, Senior Fellow at the Center for European Policy Analysis think tank. “You could go two, maybe three years,” said Cattler, a former top NATO intelligence official. In any case, other options are available in an emergency. NATO held its first-ever virtual summit in February 2022, after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Pope Leo helps Argentines embrace Francis, the pontiff who once divided them
articles.content: BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (AP) — Vast crowds of young Argentines, a generation that Catholic leaders had feared was abandoning the pews, packed the parks of Buenos Aires and cheered as if at a concert when Pope Leo XIV promised a church open to “todos, todos, todos” — everyone, everyone, everyone. Those words, like all of Leo’s surest applause lines during the visit, belonged to his Argentine predecessor, Pope Francis. So did much of the week’s adulation. Francis’ fierce defense of the downtrodden made him a moral voice abroad but long embroiled him in political fights at home — controversy that many believe deterred him from returning as pope. More than a year after his death, the more measured Leo made the homecoming Francis never could, carrying on his legacy and helping Argentines embrace their once-polarizing pope as a unifying national figure. “It’s as though it has finally become clear that Francis left a very important legacy, not just for Argentina but for the universal church,” said Pablo Forni, a sociologist at Argentina’s national research council, Conicet. “Leo is reaping what Francis sowed.” Billboards welcoming Leo bore Francis’ face. Pilgrims waved signs declaring “Francisco y León, un solo corazón” — Francis and Leo, one heart. Even libertarian President Javier Milei, who once insulted Francis as “the representative of evil on earth,” declared Francis “the most important Argentine in history” at Leo’s welcome ceremony, bringing a packed hall of his political allies and foes to its feet. Pope Leo XIV shakes hands with Argentina’s President Javier Milei as he meets authorities, civil society and the diplomatic corps at Palacio Libertad in Buenos Aires, on the third day of his twelve-day apostolic journey to South America, Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. (AP Photo/Andrew Medichini) Pope Leo XIV shakes hands with Argentina’s President Javier Milei as he meets authorities, civil society and the diplomatic corps at Palacio Libertad in Buenos Aires, on the third day of his twelve-day apostolic journey to South America, Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. (AP Photo/Andrew Medichini) As archbishop of Buenos Aires, Francis — then Jorge Mario Bergoglio — mobilized the church during Argentina’s 2001 economic crisis, sending priests into the slums and opening soup kitchens, schools and drug rehab centers as state services receded. But his concern for the poor did not make him a natural ally of Peronism, the long-dominant populist movement emphasizing social justice. He accused its leaders of arrogance and clashed with them over same-sex marriage. Yet once Francis moved to Rome as pontiff, Peronists became some of his biggest fans, seeing their priorities reflected in his criticism of unbridled capitalism and his outreach to the marginalized. That affinity infuriated conservatives, who blame Peronism for ruining Argentina’s economy and presiding over rampant corruption. However hard Francis tried to stay above the fray, even his smallest gestures — a dour expression beside right-leaning President Mauricio Macri, a relaxed lunch with left-leaning President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner — were read as proof of his political sympathies. Pope Francis and Argentina’s president Mauricio Macri pose for a picture during a private audience at the Vatican, Feb. 27, 2016. (L’Osservatore Romano/Pool Photo via AP) Pope Francis and Argentina’s president Mauricio Macri pose for a picture during a private audience at the Vatican, Feb. 27, 2016. (L’Osservatore Romano/Pool Photo via AP) A homecoming would have meant treading a minefield. Francis visited more than 60 countries as pope, including four of Argentina’s five neighbors, but never returned home, despite invitations from four successive presidents. “At first many people were thrilled to see an Argentine elected pope. But once they heard his criticism, they stopped loving him quite so much,” said the Rev. Lorenzo de Vedia, known as Padre Toto, one of the so-called slum priests who worked under Bergoglio in the capital’s informal settlements. “He became seen as a partisan pope.” Argentines weren’t the only ones Francis provoked. His blunt, freewheeling papacy divided Catholics worldwide. He accused Vatican officials of “spiritual Alzheimer’s” and called attacks from American conservatives “an honor.” He delighted progressives by opening long-taboo debates, then disappointed them by balking at doctrinal change. Now Leo — a Chicago-born former missionary in Peru whom Francis made a bishop and then a cardinal — is carrying the same causes forward with a gentleness that tempers his predecessor’s hard-charging style, church leaders say. “Francis opened the way. He broke down walls. He was forceful and impetuous, firm in his principles and startling in his proposals,” said Cardinal Pedro Barreto, a Peruvian Jesuit and close ally of Francis. “Leo XIV is clearing the path Francis laid out so that it can be traveled by every baptized member of the church.” Pope Leo XIV arrives to lead a youth prayer vigil at Monumento de los Españoles in Buenos Aires, on the fifth day of his twelve-day apostolic journey to South America, Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (AP Photo/Andrew Medichini) Pope Leo XIV arrives to lead a youth prayer vigil at Monumento de los Españoles in Buenos Aires, on the fifth day of his twelve-day apostolic journey to South America, Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (AP Photo/Andrew Medichini) Leo called the trip “a homage” to Francis, and over four days he followed in his predecessor’s footsteps: praying in Francis’ old cathedral, dispensing blessings at the prison where Francis once washed inmates’ feet, embracing residents of a disability care home where he also preached and celebrating Mass at the Luján shrine he revered. Leo invoked Francis at least 26 times. “Leo is fulfilling the promise that Francis left unfinished,” said Carlos Custer, a former Argentine ambassador to the Vatican. “Francis’ presence was felt at every turn.” But Leo did more than honor Francis’ memory. In his own voice, and without the baggage of an Argentine passport, he revived the appeals that had made Francis at once beloved and divisive at home. Pope Leo XIV, greets Marta Torres during his meeting with the staff and residents of the Pequeño Cottolengo Don Orione in Claypole, Argentina, on the fourth day of his twelve-day apostolic journey to South America, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. (AP Photo/Andrew Medichini) Pope Leo XIV, greets Marta Torres during his meeting with the staff and residents of the Pequeño Cottolengo Don Orione in Claypole, Argentina, on the fourth day of his twelve-day apostolic journey to South America, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. (AP Photo/Andrew Medichini) In Córdoba, Leo urged Argentines to keep “making a mess,” echoing Francis’ famous call for young Catholics to shake things up in their dioceses. Before an audience of garbage pickers and business leaders, he invoked Francis’ “three Ts” — tierra, techo y trabajo, or land, housing and work — the rallying cry of Argentina’s popular movements. And in his opening address to political leaders last Sunday, standing beside a self-declared “anarcho-capitalist” president known for aggressive verbal outbursts and harsh austerity measures, he urged “careful use of words” and insisted that “the economy must be at the service of the person, not the person in the service of the economy.” “There is continuity between them in every respect — in their message of peace, their love for the poor, their choice to go places where people are suffering, in their emotional connection to the people,” said the Rev. Carlos María Galli, a prominent Argentine theologian who was close to Francis. “Francis brought Leo to the center of the church, and Leo has now brought Francis back to us.” Pope Leo XIV, accompanied by Buenos Aires Archbishop Jorge Ignacio Garcia Cuerva, visits the federal prison complex in Buenos Aires, on the sixth day of his twelve-day apostolic journey to South America, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Andrew Medichini) Pope Leo XIV, accompanied by Buenos Aires Archbishop Jorge Ignacio Garcia Cuerva, visits the federal prison complex in Buenos Aires, on the sixth day of his twelve-day apostolic journey to South America, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Andrew Medichini) Politicians scrambled to claim Leo’s message as their own. Axel Kicillof, the Peronist governor of Buenos Aires province and a leading opposition figure, hailed the visit as “very necessary in these times of cruelty.” Vice President Victoria Villarruel defended the concept of social justice derided by her boss and championed by Francis, blaming “ignorance and fanaticism” for its frequent association with Peronism. Even Milei’s spokesman, Adrián Ravier, insisted Wednesday that by taming inflation, the government had put “the economy at the service of people.” For observers, that political jockeying proved the wisdom of Francis’ decision to stay away — and the value of Leo as his messenger. “Had Bergoglio said the same things and visited the same places, it would have been seen as far more political,” said Gustavo Morello, an Argentine sociologist of religion at Boston College. “But you can’t accuse Leo of being a Peronist. So when he speaks about workers or people with disabilities, it’s the church speaking ... and if you don’t like it, you can take it up with God.” Pope Leo XIV prays in front of a plaque commemorating Pope Francis prior to the start of a vespers service at the Metropolitan Cathedral of the Most Holy Trinity in Buenos Aires, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026.(AP Photo/Andrew Medichini, Pool) Pope Leo XIV prays in front of a plaque commemorating Pope Francis prior to the start of a vespers service at the Metropolitan Cathedral of the Most Holy Trinity in Buenos Aires, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026.(AP Photo/Andrew Medichini, Pool) Associated Press writer Mauricio Savarese in Lima, Peru, contributed to this report.
